q-94154:
We're given that $Z∼N(0,1),$ and we wish to compute $P(Z\ge 2.11).$ The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069404/assets/1d2d207ca7c72b0e4ee5a8b34c0f48f288a104de643ab552ccbfec15dbd08fcf.png)

By the definition of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z),$ 

$$
P(Z\le z)=Φ(z).
$$

Since the total area under the graph equals $1,$ we can express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge 2.11) & =1-P(Z<2.11) \\  & =1-Φ(2.11)\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069404/assets/0e0d5909a42ae2ee25dbee577b68fa0c6aef45285b6157f610d5629b227c2752.png)

From the table, we know that

$$
Φ(2.11)=0.9826.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge 2.11) & =1-Φ(2.11) \\  & =1-0.9826 \\  & =0.0174.\end{aligned}
$$

q-131521:
We're given that $Z∼N(0,1),$ and we wish to compute $P(-1.99<Z<-0.99).$ The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069404/assets/8dc66c8ceed4366688dc040104eaece3d251ecb9f72d9aae0827ead3fe933570.png)

By the definition of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z),$ 

$$
P(Z\le z)=Φ(z).
$$

So, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.99<Z<-0.99) & =P(Z<-0.99)-P(Z\le -1.99) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.99)-P(Z\le -1.99) \\  & =Φ(-0.99)-Φ(-1.99).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.99) & =0.0233 \\ Φ(-0.99) & =0.1611\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.99<Z<-0.99) & =Φ(-0.99)-Φ(-1.99) \\  & =0.1611-0.0233 \\  & =0.1378.\end{aligned}
$$

q-94194:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069404/assets/46b71217fcee1d130b3778ce2cd101aac9814870b71683656987d476e71412c1.png)

By the definition of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z),$ 

$$
P(Z\le z)=Φ(z).
$$

So, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.2<Z<-0.31) & =P(Z<-0.31)-P(Z\le -1.2) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.31)-P(Z\le -1.2) \\  & =Φ(-0.31)-Φ(-1.2)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.2) & =0.1151 \\ Φ(-0.31) & =0.3783\end{aligned}

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.2<Z<-0.31) & =Φ(-0.31)-Φ(-1.2) \\  & =0.3783-0.1151 \\  & =0.2632.\end{aligned}
$$

q-96728:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial,  we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(4,0.2),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x})(0.2)^{x}(0.8)^{4-x}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =f(3) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{3})(0.2)^{3}(0.8)^{4-3} \\  & =4(0.2)^{3}(0.8) \\  & ≈0.0256\end{aligned}
$$

to $4$ decimal places.

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}

$$

q-97521:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(7,0.5),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.5)^{x}(0.5)^{7-x}.
$$

Computing $P(X\le 6)$ will require us to compute $f(x)$ at $x=0,1,2,…,6.$ However, if we compute the complement $P(X>6)$ instead, then we will only have to compute $f(x)$ at $x=7,$ which will result in a much faster computation.

Computing $P(X>6),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>6) & =P(X\in {7}) \\  & =f(7) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{7})(0.5)^{7}(0.5)^{7-7} \\  & =(0.5)^{7} \\  & ≈0.0078\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 6) & =1-P(X>6) \\  & ≈1-0.0078 \\  & =0.9922\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

q-134529:
Recall that when $n$ is a positive integer, 

$$
(1+x)^{n}=1+nx+\frac{1}{2!}n(n-1){x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{n}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1+x)}^{6} & =1+6x+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 6\cdot 5\cdot {x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{n} \\  & =1+6x+15{x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for small $x,$ we have

$$
{(1+x)}^{6}≈1+6x+15{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, we substitute $x=-0.1$ into the above approximation of $(1+x)^{6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0.9)^{6} & =(1+(-0.1))^{6} \\  & ≈1+6(-0.1)+15(-0.1)^{2} \\  & =1-6(0.1)+15(0.01) \\  & =1-0.6+0.15 \\  & =0.55\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using a calculator, we can compute the percentage error, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}%\,error & =\frac{\text{amount of error}}{\text{exact value}}\times 100 \\  & =\frac{|(0.9)^{6}-0.55|}{(0.9)^{6}}\times 100 \\  & ≈3.49%\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

q-134649:
The binomial theorem for positive integer $n$ states that

$$
(a+b)^{n}=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{0}){a}^{n}{b}^{0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{1}){a}^{n-1}{b}^{1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{2}){a}^{n-2}{b}^{2}+…+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{n}){a}^{0}{b}^{n}.
$$

By substituting $a=4,$ $b=x,$ and $n=5,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(4+x)}^{5} & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0}){(4)}^{5}{(x)}^{0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1}){(4)}^{5-1}{(x)}^{1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2}){(4)}^{5-2}{(x)}^{2}+⋯ \\  & =1{(4)}^{5}+5{(4)}^{4}{(x)}^{1}+10{(4)}^{3}{(x)}^{2}+⋯ \\  & =1\,024+5(256)(x)+10(64)({x}^{2})+⋯ \\  & =1\,024+1\,280x+640{x}^{2}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for small $x,$ we have

$$
{(4+x)}^{5}≈1\,024+1\,280x+640{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=-0.11$ into the above approximation of $(4+x)^{5}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3.89)^{5} & =(4+(-0.11))^{5} \\  & ≈1\,024+1\,280(-0.11)+640(-0.11)^{2} \\  & =1\,024-1\,280(0.11)+640(0.012\,1) \\  & =1\,024-140.8+7.744 \\  & =890.944,\end{aligned}
$$

to three decimal places.

q-162704:
Let $P$ be the matrix that represents the rotation, $Q$ be the matrix that represents the stretching, and $R$ be the matrix that represents the reflection. These are given by the following elementary transformation matrices:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Hence, the combined transformation can be represented by the matrix $RQP:$

$$
\begin{aligned}RQP & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
$a+b=(-3)+1=-2.$

q-89366:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the spinner lands on red or green.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=12$ spins

- the probability of landing on red or green on any spin is

$$
p=\frac{3}{10}+\frac{3}{10}=\frac{3}{5}
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(12,\frac{3}{5}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=5$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{5}){(\frac{3}{5})}^{5}{(1-\frac{3}{5})}^{12-5} \\  & =\frac{12!}{5!(12-5)!}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{7} \\  & =792{(\frac{3}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{7} \\  & =0.101\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

q-130744:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of left-handed students in the group.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=8$ students in the group

- the probability of a student being left-handed is $p=0.175$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(8,0.175).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{x}){(0.175)}^{x}{(1-0.175)}^{8-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{x}){(0.175)}^{x}{(0.825)}^{8-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that at least $6$ students are left-handed. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 6) & =P(X=6)+P(X=7)+P(X=8) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{6}){(0.175)}^{6}{(0.825)}^{8-6}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{7}){(0.175)}^{7}{(0.825)}^{8-7}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{8}){(0.175)}^{8}{(0.825)}^{8-8} \\  & =28{(0.175)}^{6}{(0.825)}^{2}+8{(0.175)}^{7}{(0.825)}^{1}+1{(0.175)}^{8}{(0.825)}^{0} \\  & ≈0.0006\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

q-84805:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of balloons that pop.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=15$ balloons

- the probability that one balloon pops is $p=\frac{1}{5}$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(15,\frac{1}{5}).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{x}){(\frac{1}{5})}^{x}{(1-\frac{1}{5})}^{15-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{x}){(\frac{1}{5})}^{x}{(\frac{4}{5})}^{15-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability of getting at least $3$ balloons that pop. This corresponds to $P(X>2).$

However, computing

$$
P(X>2)=P(X=3)+P(X=4)+…+P(X=10)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>2) & =1-P(X\le 2) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{0}){(\frac{1}{5})}^{0}{(\frac{4}{5})}^{15-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{1}){(\frac{1}{5})}^{1}{(\frac{4}{5})}^{15-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{2}){(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}{(\frac{4}{5})}^{15-2}] \\  & =1-[{(\frac{4}{5})}^{15}+15(\frac{1}{5}){(\frac{4}{5})}^{14}+105{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}{(\frac{4}{5})}^{13}] \\  & =1-0.398\,023 \\  & =0.602\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

q-84804:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of works of art sold.
Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=14$ works of art

- the probability of selling each work is $p=35%=0.35$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(14,0.35).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{14}{x})(0.35)^{x}(1-0.35)^{14-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{14}{x})(0.35)^{x}(0.65)^{14-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that the painter sells $2$ or more works of art. This corresponds to $P(X\ge 2).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\ge 2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+…+P(X=14)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{14}{0})(0.35)^{0}(0.65)^{14-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{14}{1})(0.35)^{1}(0.65)^{14-1}] \\  & =1-[(0.65)^{14}+14(0.35)(0.65)^{13}] \\  & =1-0.020\,519 \\  & =0.979\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
